title: Technical deep dive - Private (on-prem) observability + SIEM forwarding
summary: NorthBridge (regulated financial) asked for a deep dive on Redwood Private observability in an on-prem / constrained-egress environment. Focus was on what Redwood includes by default (dashboards + alerts + log pipeline defaults), what is required for a "supported" install, and how logs/audit signals can be forwarded to their SIEM (Splunk HTTP Event Collector) with tight controls (no outbound internet, internal PKI, RBAC, evidence/audit requirements). Redwood walked through the minimum observability pack approach (Prometheus + Grafana provisioning optional; compatible with customer-managed Prometheus/Grafana), default alert philosophy (SLO burn + pipeline health), log schema and redaction, and air-gapped packaging patterns (offline bundles, image mirroring). Customer flagged concerns about log volume/cost, label cardinality, and how upgrades affect alert rules/dashboards.
topics: On-prem constraints (air-gapped, internal PKI, no external egress)
Supported backends: Prometheus/Grafana and customer-managed equivalents
Dashboards included by default (gateway/API, runtime prefill/decode, GPU, control plane, installer health)
Alerting approach (SLO burn-rate, severity mapping, noise controls, rule loading checks)
SIEM forwarding: structured logs, redaction, sampling, and Splunk HEC integration
Audit logging expectations for Grafana and rule changes
action_items: Redwood (Kevin) to send example Vector/Fluent Bit configs for forwarding structured logs to Splunk HEC with mTLS + index routing.
Redwood (Sergio) to share current dashboard catalog list and required metrics/labels for each dashboard.
Redwood (Markus) to provide air-gapped packaging notes: offline bundle layout, image mirroring steps, and minimal dependencies list.
Customer (Ravi) to confirm Splunk HEC endpoint requirements (TLS/mTLS, token handling, allowed cipher suites) and retention policy constraints for LLM logs.
Customer (Alicia) to share their preferred Prometheus/Grafana deployment pattern (OpenShift monitoring stack vs standalone) and any restrictions on Grafana provisioning APIs.
next_steps: Schedule 45-min follow-up to review Redwood "supported signals" checklist against NorthBridge go-live checklist.
NorthBridge to identify target on-prem cluster type for PoC (OpenShift vs upstream k8s) and whether GPUs are NVIDIA A100 or L40S.
Redwood to provide a sample "day-1" runbook excerpt: validating metrics ingestion, rule load status, and log pipeline health.
transcript:
Meeting Header
Recorded: 2025-01-29 19:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Title: Technical deep dive - Private (on-prem) observability + SIEM forwarding

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Markus Klein, Kevin Osei, Sergio Costa
NorthBridge Financial Group: Alicia Chen, Ravi Menon, Diane Kessler, Tomás Ibarra

---

[00:00] Liam (Redwood): Cool. Thanks everyone. This is Liam. I’m the TAM-ish point of contact on the Redwood side. Today is basically a technical deep dive on the Private observability bundle we include, specifically for on-prem and your SIEM requirements.

[00:18] Alicia (Customer): Yep. Thanks. Our main concern is we can’t do any outbound internet. It’s… essentially air-gapped with like controlled proxies, but assume no egress. And we have a hard requirement that logs go to Splunk, and metrics go into Prometheus we run.

[00:33] Markus (Redwood): Great. That’s exactly the lane. I’m Markus, I run Solutions for Private deployments. We’ve been standardizing an “observability minimum pack” for Private because we kept seeing bespoke installs. So the pitch is: day-one usable dashboards, a baseline set of alerts, and log pipeline defaults that are safe by default.

[00:56] Diane (Customer): Can I just ask right away: when you say you “include dashboards,” does that mean you’re shipping Grafana? Or you’re shipping JSON we import? We have restrictions on running extra stuff.

[01:08] Sergio (Redwood): Yeah, good question. It’s flexible. We can integrate with customer-managed Grafana/Prometheus, or optionally deploy a “small” Grafana instance if you want. The minimum pack is basically: Grafana dashboards (as provisioned files), Prometheus rules (PrometheusRule style), and logging agent configs (Vector or Fluent Bit).

[01:26] Tomás (Customer): We’re OpenShift in the data center. We can deploy operators, but we’d rather reuse the existing monitoring stack if it’s compatible.

[01:35] Sergio (Redwood): OpenShift is common. If you already have Prometheus + Grafana, we’ll target those. The key is the metrics contract: metric names and labels, and that the rules parse.

[01:47] Ravi (Customer): SIEM side: Splunk HEC. We require mTLS and we want structured JSON with redaction. We do not want prompts in logs. We also need audit trails: who changed dashboards, who changed alert rules, access to Grafana, that sort of thing.

[02:05] Kevin (Redwood): I’m Kevin, I own audit log export and SIEM integration pieces. On the prompt logging: the defaults are designed not to log sensitive payloads. We use structured logs with fields like request_id, tenant, route, model, status, error_code, latency buckets, and we can include token counts. But not prompt text by default.

[02:26] Alicia (Customer): That’s a big one. We’ve had vendors “accidentally” log request bodies.

[02:30] Kevin (Redwood): Totally. And we’ll call that out explicitly in docs: safe-by-default, plus redaction filters in the collector.

[02:38] Liam (Redwood): Maybe we start with what’s included by default, and then we drill into on-prem packaging and SIEM forwarding.

[02:46] Alicia (Customer): Sounds good.

[02:49] Sergio (Redwood): Ok. Dashboards first. In the minimum pack we have:
- Gateway / API overview: RPS, p50/p95/p99 latency, 4xx/5xx, streaming disconnect rates.
- Runtime performance: prefill vs decode latency, queue depth, batch sizes, KV cache hit rate.
- GPU saturation: utilization, memory use, throttling / power limit signals.
- Routing / fallback behavior: percent served by primary vs fallback model variant, region/cluster routing decisions (for private, it’s usually pool-level).
- Control plane health: policy/config store, auth integration health, internal service errors.
- “Private install health”: installer/upgrade controller, component readiness, and rule loading status.

[03:35] Diane (Customer): Do you also have a dashboard for “missing metrics”? We get burned by dashboards that just show blank and nobody knows why.

[03:42] Sergio (Redwood): Yes. We have a “missing signals” section plus alerts. Like if Prometheus isn’t scraping runtime metrics endpoints, or if the log collector is dropping logs.

[03:53] Tomás (Customer): How do you keep the label cardinality sane? If you have tenant + route + model, that can explode.

[04:02] Sergio (Redwood): We constrain it. For example, route is a bounded set of endpoints, model is a bounded set of deployed models. Tenant is the tricky one; in Private we recommend using a stable tenant_id that is low-ish cardinality (like business unit), not per-user. And we do not put request_id as a label. Request_id stays in logs/traces.

[04:25] Diane (Customer): So you’re not doing exemplars / traces in the minimum pack?

[04:29] Sergio (Redwood): Tracing is optional. We don’t want to force a tracing backend for the minimum. But we can emit OpenTelemetry spans and you can wire that if you have it. For the baseline “supported” bar, it’s metrics + logs.

[04:44] Alicia (Customer): Ok. Alerts: what exactly do you ship? We’re sensitive to noise. We do not want pager storms for “GPU 80%” kind of stuff.

[04:53] Markus (Redwood): Same. The alert philosophy is basically: SLO burn for availability/latency, plus a few hard failure alerts.

[05:01] Sergio (Redwood): Right. Categories:
1) Availability / error rate: e.g. 5xx spikes, or “request success ratio” burning the SLO.
2) Latency: p95/p99 above SLO, burn-rate style with multi-window.
3) Saturation: queue depth building, GPU memory exhaustion signals, CPU/mem/disk pressure if you run components on shared nodes.
4) Pipeline health: Prometheus scrape failures, rule evaluation errors, collector backlog/drops, exporter failures.
5) Control plane: config/policy store errors, auth integration failing.

[05:36] Ravi (Customer): Rule evaluation errors is a big one. We had an incident where rules silently stopped evaluating because of a syntax change.

[05:44] Sergio (Redwood): Yep, we include an alert on rule load failures and promtool validation in CI on our side. Also we’re adding a post-install validation command in the installer to check rule group status.

[05:59] Diane (Customer): When you say “post-install validation command” what is that in practice?

[06:04] Markus (Redwood): The installer outputs a report. It checks: can we reach Grafana API (if used), are dashboards provisioned, are metrics endpoints scrapeable, and are Prometheus rules loaded without errors. For air-gapped, it’s all local.

[06:21] Alicia (Customer): That’s good. We need a go-live checklist. We call it “supported signals” or “operational readiness.”

[06:27] Liam (Redwood): We have a “supported signals” checklist we can share. It maps required signals to queries and pass/fail.

[06:36] Ravi (Customer): SIEM: what are your “structured logs”? Like a schema? We don’t want random strings.

[06:43] Kevin (Redwood): We do JSON logs. Typical fields:
- timestamp
- severity
- service (gateway/runtime/control-plane)
- environment
- cluster
- tenant_id
- route
- model
- request_id
- trace_id (if present)
- status_code
- error_code (Redwood-defined enums)
- latency_ms (sometimes split into queue_ms, prefill_ms, decode_ms)
- tokens_in / tokens_out
- cache_hit (boolean-ish)
Plus a message string for humans.

[07:19] Ravi (Customer): And you can guarantee no prompt text?

[07:22] Kevin (Redwood): Default is no prompt text. We also have a redaction filter so if an upstream component accidentally logs something in a field we don’t expect, the collector can drop or hash. But yes, we’re designing it so prompt and completion payloads are not in logs.

[07:40] Alicia (Customer): What about audit logs? For example, if someone changes an alert rule in Prometheus, or changes a dashboard in Grafana.

[07:49] Kevin (Redwood): For Grafana specifically: if it’s customer-managed Grafana, you use Grafana’s own audit logging (Enterprise has more features; OSS has some logs). In our docs we describe what to enable and what to ship to SIEM: login events, dashboard changes, datasource changes, API token usage.

[08:10] Ravi (Customer): We’re Grafana Enterprise already.

[08:12] Kevin (Redwood): Perfect. Then you can enable audit logs in Grafana and forward those. For Prometheus rule changes, it depends how you manage config. If you’re GitOps (Argo, etc), the audit trail is in Git + cluster audit logs. We also log installer actions: “applied rule bundle version X,” “provisioned dashboards version Y,” that kind of thing.

[08:36] Tomás (Customer): On-prem packaging: we can’t pull images from Docker Hub. Everything has to be mirrored to our internal registry. How do you handle that? Is it a separate bundle?

[08:47] Markus (Redwood): Yes. We have an air-gapped mode. The pack artifacts (dashboards, rules, logging configs) can be delivered as an offline bundle. The installer can take a local path. For container images like Vector/Fluent Bit or Grafana (if you choose to deploy it), those get mirrored to your internal registry. We provide a list of images + digests.

[09:12] Diane (Customer): Is Vector required? We already run Fluent Bit in the cluster.

[09:16] Kevin (Redwood): Not required. We support Vector and Fluent Bit as the “recommended collectors.” If you already have Fluent Bit, we can provide a config snippet: parse JSON logs, add a few fields, route to Splunk HEC, and apply sampling.

[09:32] Ravi (Customer): Sampling: talk to me about sampling. We cannot ship every request log if you’re doing high QPS.

[09:38] Kevin (Redwood): Totally. We provide knobs for:
- sampling by route (e.g., health checks sampled heavily)
- sampling by status_code (keep 5xx at 100%, sample 2xx at 1-5%)
- rate limits per service
- drop noisy fields
Also we recommend metrics for the high-volume stuff (latency distributions, token counts) so you’re not using logs for performance analytics.

[10:08] Alicia (Customer): That’s aligned. We use Splunk mostly for incident forensics and compliance evidence, not for p99 graphs.

[10:15] Sergio (Redwood): Exactly. The dashboards are metrics-driven. Logs are for drill-down by request_id or error_code.

[10:24] Diane (Customer): What about retention guidance? We’ve got short retention for hot logs, longer for audit logs.

[10:30] Kevin (Redwood): We’ll give default guidance: operational logs short (like 7-14 days hot), audit logs longer (like 90+ depending on policy). But we don’t enforce retention; it’s your backend.

[10:46] Ravi (Customer): For Splunk HEC, we require mTLS. Does Fluent Bit support that? And does Redwood’s config cover it?

[10:54] Kevin (Redwood): Yes, Fluent Bit supports TLS and can be configured with client certs. Vector too. We’ll send both example configs. The main thing is secret handling: certs and tokens in Kubernetes Secrets, mounted read-only, RBAC locked down.

[11:15] Tomás (Customer): On RBAC: do you ship cluster roles? We’re least privilege and security reviews are brutal.

[11:22] Markus (Redwood): We ship minimal RBAC. For dashboards/rules provisioning, it’s usually namespace-scoped. For scraping metrics, Prometheus needs access to endpoints; if you have a cluster monitoring operator, it already has patterns. We’ll document the exact permissions.

[11:42] Alicia (Customer): Can we turn off Grafana provisioning? We don’t want an installer pushing into Grafana via API. That’s a change control problem.

[11:51] Sergio (Redwood): Yes. You can run “export mode” where we just render the dashboards and you import via your pipeline. Same with rules. But the default is provisioning because it reduces day-one issues.

[12:07] Diane (Customer): If we do import ourselves, are the dashboards versioned? Like, can we pin to a version and track changes?

[12:12] Sergio (Redwood): Yes. Everything is versioned as a bundle. Dashboards have stable UIDs, folder naming conventions, and release notes for changes.

[12:25] Liam (Redwood): Maybe pause and ask: what’s your current monitoring stack exactly? You mentioned Prometheus and Grafana Enterprise.

[12:32] Alicia (Customer): We have Prometheus Operator in OpenShift, plus Grafana Enterprise, plus Splunk for logs. Some teams also use Elastic for app logs but we’re standardizing on Splunk. We’re not using Grafana Cloud.

[12:48] Diane (Customer): Alerting routes through PagerDuty for sev1/sev2. But we want a “burn rate” style approach, not static thresholds. We have error budget policy.

[12:57] Sergio (Redwood): Perfect. We align. We have burn-rate rules with multiple window pairs (like 5m/1h and 30m/6h style) so it’s both fast detection and sustained issues.

[13:10] Diane (Customer): Nice. And severity mapping?

[13:13] Sergio (Redwood): We label rules with severity: page vs ticket. Critical availability and hard failures are page. Saturation tends to be ticket unless it’s causing SLO burn.

[13:28] Ravi (Customer): Do you have a way to detect “collector is dropping logs”? Because we’ve had that where the agent CPU throttles and silently drops.

[13:37] Kevin (Redwood): Yes. We ship metrics from the collector: dropped events, retry counts, backlog queue depth, export errors. We include alerts on that.

[13:52] Tomás (Customer): Is that collector metrics in Prometheus?

[13:55] Kevin (Redwood): Yes. Either via a /metrics endpoint or sidecar metrics depending on the collector.

[14:04] Alicia (Customer): Air-gapped again: if we can’t pull Helm charts, how do you deliver it?

[14:09] Markus (Redwood): Offline chart bundle. You’ll get a tarball with charts + values templates + dashboard JSON + rule YAML + log configs, plus a manifest of images with digests. Your process mirrors images; then you run installer with “--airgap-bundle /path/to/bundle.”

[14:32] Diane (Customer): Upgrades: how likely is it that a Redwood upgrade breaks our dashboards or rules?

[14:37] Sergio (Redwood): We try hard to keep metric names stable. When we add metrics, no big deal. When we change semantics, we version it and document it. The observability pack itself has its own version, and we maintain a compatibility matrix with installer versions.

[14:58] Alicia (Customer): We’ll need that matrix in writing.

[15:01] Markus (Redwood): Yep.

[15:03] Ravi (Customer): Also, how do you handle “tenant” in a regulated environment? We’re multi-tenant internally. But we do not want one business unit seeing another’s logs or dashboards.

[15:15] Liam (Redwood): For Private, you can either run separate clusters, or use RBAC at the observability layer. Grafana can do folder permissions, Prometheus can do multi-tenancy with separate instances or with a layer like Mimir, but we’re not requiring that. For logs, Splunk indexes can be separated.

[15:37] Ravi (Customer): We do separate indexes per environment and BU.

[15:40] Kevin (Redwood): Great. Then collector routing can send different tenants to different indexes based on tenant_id field.

[15:48] Alicia (Customer): Ok, now specifically: what dashboards and alerts do you include “by default” in Private? I need to communicate to our leadership that we’re not building this from scratch.

[15:59] Sergio (Redwood): By default (minimum pack): those six dashboard families I listed. Roughly 12-15 dashboards total, depending on whether you enable the control plane ones. Alerts: SLO burn for availability and latency, plus critical error rate, plus pipeline health, plus resource exhaustion (GPU memory, disk pressure for the components).

[16:24] Diane (Customer): Can we see a screenshot or a wireframe?

[16:27] Sergio (Redwood): Yes, we can share wireframes and a catalog list. I’ll send the catalog with panel inventory.

[16:34] Tomás (Customer): Technical question: for GPU utilization, are you relying on DCGM exporter or nvidia-smi scraping? We already run DCGM.

[16:44] Sergio (Redwood): DCGM exporter is preferred. We integrate with those metrics. If you already have it, we just reference the standard metric names. For on-prem it’s often already there.

[16:59] Diane (Customer): Runtime metrics: do you provide histograms? We like histograms for latency.

[17:04] Sergio (Redwood): Yes, we expose histograms for request duration and can split into prefill/decode with separate histos depending on runtime config. Some of that depends on version but that’s the direction.

[17:21] Alicia (Customer): One more: do you log model names? That can be sensitive.

[17:26] Kevin (Redwood): We can control that. Model identifier can be an internal alias. Default is model name as configured in Redwood, but you can set it to a sanitized ID.

[17:40] Ravi (Customer): Good. And request_id: we like to correlate across systems. Do you also propagate trace headers?

[17:46] Kevin (Redwood): We propagate request_id and can propagate W3C traceparent if you enable it.

[17:56] Diane (Customer): Ok.

[18:00] Liam (Redwood): I want to make sure we address the “supported” question. For Private, what does Redwood support mean here? It means: you have the minimum signals wired, and the dashboards/alerts load without errors. We’ll give you a checklist to validate.

[18:17] Alicia (Customer): That’s what we need. We have a go-live gate.

[18:22] Ravi (Customer): For compliance we also need evidence. Like, “these dashboards exist, these alerts exist, these audits are enabled.”

[18:31] Kevin (Redwood): We can produce a post-install report that enumerates what was installed and versions. You can attach that to your change record.

[18:42] Tomás (Customer): Is this report a file? JSON? Something we can archive.

[18:46] Markus (Redwood): Typically text output and also export as JSON. We can confirm exact format, but yes, exportable.

[18:58] Diane (Customer): Great.

[19:00] (cross-talk)

[19:02] Alicia (Customer): Sorry, go ahead Diane.

[19:04] Diane (Customer): Just: who owns tuning? Like, after we run in production, thresholds might be too sensitive or too lax.

[19:12] Sergio (Redwood): We provide defaults and a tuning workflow: run them in staging with load, look at expected fire rates, adjust window/threshold, and apply suppression for known maintenance windows. We’ll also recommend which alerts are “do not touch” because they indicate pipeline breakage.

[19:36] Alicia (Customer): Ok. That’s fine.

[19:39] Ravi (Customer): On Splunk tokens: we can’t store long-lived tokens in plaintext. We use Vault. Do you integrate with Vault?

[19:49] Kevin (Redwood): We don’t require Vault but we can reference secrets from external secret stores via ExternalSecrets operators. If you have that, we can plug in.

[20:03] Tomás (Customer): We do.

[20:05] Kevin (Redwood): Great.

[20:08] Liam (Redwood): Let’s talk about your on-prem constraint: truly air-gapped or controlled egress?

[20:13] Alicia (Customer): Controlled egress only for OS patching. For this platform, assume no egress. We can manually move artifacts.

[20:22] Markus (Redwood): That fits the air-gap workflow.

[20:26] Diane (Customer): Another pain: rule changes on upgrade. If we pin the pack version, can we keep rules stable while we upgrade Redwood runtime?

[20:34] Sergio (Redwood): Yes, you can pin. But if runtime metrics change, the dashboards may not be fully accurate. That’s why we keep compatibility constraints. But generally we support pinning within a supported range.

[20:52] Tomás (Customer): Does the pack depend on Kubernetes version?

[20:55] Markus (Redwood): Only minimally. Mostly it’s standard ConfigMaps, PrometheusRule resources, etc. OpenShift adds some specifics but we handle that.

[21:06] Ravi (Customer): Ok. What about “control plane health” metrics? If control plane is down, do we lose all telemetry?

[21:12] Sergio (Redwood): No. The runtime and gateway emit metrics locally. Control plane health is additional. Telemetry should continue if control plane is degraded.

[21:25] Diane (Customer): That’s good.

[21:27] Alicia (Customer): Can you confirm: you’re not asking us to use Grafana Cloud or a managed thing.

[21:31] Liam (Redwood): Correct. For Private on-prem, we assume customer-managed.

[21:36] Alicia (Customer): Great.

[21:38] (brief pause)

[21:40] Liam (Redwood): I think the key open items are: we’ll send you the catalog, sample configs for Splunk HEC, and the air-gap packaging notes. And you send us the specific Splunk constraints.

[21:54] Ravi (Customer): Yes. We’ll confirm TLS requirements and whether we want per-tenant index routing.

[22:01] Diane (Customer): And we’ll confirm whether we can allow Grafana API provisioning or if we need everything GitOps.

[22:07] Sergio (Redwood): Perfect.

[22:10] Tomás (Customer): Before we wrap, do you mention any “runbooks” as part of this? We want a day-2 guide.

[22:16] Markus (Redwood): Yes. Day-2 ops runbook: triage missing metrics, collector issues, dashboard troubleshooting, and escalation.

[22:25] Alicia (Customer): Good.

[22:27] Liam (Redwood): Ok, we’ve got the asks. I’ll recap at the end. Any last technical questions?

[22:33] Ravi (Customer): One last: do you support sending logs to object storage instead of SIEM?

[22:39] Kevin (Redwood): Yes, forwarding targets include SIEM (Splunk), object storage (S3-compatible), or a managed log backend if allowed. For you, it’s Splunk.

[22:51] Alicia (Customer): Ok.

[22:53] Liam (Redwood): Cool. We’ll follow up with the artifacts. Thanks everyone.

---

Post-call recap (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send: dashboard/alert catalog, supported signals checklist, Splunk HEC forwarding configs (Vector + Fluent Bit), air-gap packaging notes.
- Customer to send: Splunk HEC endpoint/mTLS specifics, preferred provisioning approach (API vs GitOps), retention and index routing constraints.

(End of transcript)
